summary: ORCA is an automated program repair pipeline for microservice incidents that starts from paired failure/reference telemetry (logs, traces, metrics), distills a 'fault signature', localizes code or deployment-config candidates (SBFL + config abstractor), generates diffs via bounded 'repair graph' agents with an exploration-agent fallback, and verifies patches with a four-check Telemetry-Grounded Patch Verifier. It is evaluated on an author-built 575-case benchmark (200 synthetic code, 225 synthetic config, 150 'real-incident') against six baselines.

claims.claim: On the real-incident subset ORCA yields 113 valid patches and 45 telemetry-replay mitigations vs mini-SWE-agent's 74 and 23, at ~26k vs ~640k mean tokens per case.
claims.evidence: §V-D3 text and Fig. 3 (numbers present in body). But 94 of the 150 'real' cases are mutation variants of 9 seed incidents (§V-A, §VI external threats), so only 56 are independent real incidents; manual inspection (by the authors) confirms only 31 of the 45 mitigations as fault-addressing.

claims.claim: ORCA outperforms all baselines on synthetic code and configuration faults.
claims.evidence: Table II: config subset 213/225 valid patches and 210 mitigated replays vs mini-SWE-agent 177 and 174. On TT-Java code faults only 32/100 patches are valid and compile and 30 pass tests (second best 17), and telemetry gives little signal for that fault class.

claims.claim: Outcomes are robust to LLM backbone; backbone mainly changes token cost.
claims.evidence: Table III: seven models, C1 113-127/150, C4-mitigated 37-45, tokens 6.9k-26.4k.

claims.claim: The telemetry fault signature (plus sanitized issue context) is the key ingredient.
claims.evidence: §V-H ablation removes both jointly: File hit 49->8, C1 113->40, C4 45->13. The two inputs are not ablated separately, so the telemetry contribution is not isolated from the issue text.

patterns.note: Uses observability telemetry both as repair context and as a patch-verification signal; main contribution.
Multi-axis verifier (apply, compile/test, test-oracle integrity, telemetry replay) filters patches; manual check shows replay is an imperfect oracle (31/45).
Deterministic localization stage feeds bounded single-call repair agents with an exploration fallback; cheaper than open-ended shell agent.
Reports tokens/time per case; bounded repair-graph calls ~10k median tokens vs 640k for mini-SWE-agent.
Backbone sensitivity shows cheap models (GPT-4o-mini) match expensive ones inside a constrained pipeline (Table III).
Explicitly departs from SWE-bench issue-to-patch framing; new author-built benchmark.

[retag 2026-10-07] ORCA is a fixed pipeline: telemetry fault signature -> SBFL/config localization -> deterministic dispatcher (Alg. 1) -> bounded single-call repair-graph agents -> exploration-agent fallback -> 4-check verifier. Vs the open mini-SWE-agent loop on the same model (DeepSeek-V4-pro, T=0) with the same fault signature: real incidents 113 vs 74 valid patches, 45 vs 23 telemetry mitigations, 26k vs 640k tokens/case (§V-D3, Fig. 3); synthetic config 213 vs 177 valid at ~1/3 the tokens; TT-Java 30 vs 17 test-passing (Table II). Caveats: author-built 575-case benchmark, single run, baseline lacks ORCA's SBFL localization, and 123/200 synthetic code cases fall back to the exploration loop.

methodology.sample: 575 cases: 200 synthetic code (100 Python Online Boutique, 100 Java Train-Ticket), 225 synthetic config (4 testbeds), 150 'real-incident' (56 reproduced from 4 OSS repos + 94 mutation variants from 9 seeds).
methodology.baselines: Direct, One-Shot (fed ORCA's own top-5 localization), ReAct capped at 8 steps, Agentless and AutoCodeRover (Python-only, so run on a subset), mini-SWE-agent; all at temperature 0 and low reasoning effort. All baselines receive ORCA's fault signature.
methodology.models: DeepSeek-V4-pro for RQ1; seven backbones in RQ2 (DeepSeek-V4-pro/Flash, Claude-Opus-4.8, GPT-5.1, GPT-5-mini, GPT-4o-mini, Qwen3-Coder-30B).
methodology.variance: Main results single run at T=0; temperature study uses 3 seeds for generation metrics but telemetry replay measured once per temperature.
methodology.ablations: Joint removal of fault signature + issue context; Exploration-agent run count N in {1,3,5}.
methodology.contamination_controls: Benchmark bundles sanitized of issue/PR ids, repair titles, ground-truth paths; upstream fixes of public OSS repos may still be in training data (not discussed).
methodology.languages: Synthetic: Python and Java; real-incident subset spans eight source languages plus Dockerfiles, YAML, .env, Makefiles.

standards.artifacts: Benchmark 'will be made publicly available'; no code or data link in the text.

biases.detail: Authors built the benchmark, the verifier (TGPV) and its C4 metric, and the manual 'fault-addressing' labels used to validate C4.
ReAct capped at 8 steps and all baselines at low reasoning effort; Agentless/AutoCodeRover only run on Python cases; mini-SWE-agent given an SWE-bench-style prompt rather than a telemetry-tuned one.
Telemetry replay can credit patches that just suppress telemetry emission; 14 of 45 replay mitigations were not confirmed as repairs, and the case study's 'fix' disables instrumentation.
'Real-incident' subset has only 56 independent incidents; 94 are mutations of 9 seeds, inflating apparent N.
Code and benchmark not released at time of writing.
Headline comparisons are single T=0 runs with no CIs.

coi.affiliations: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology; University of Toronto.
coi.detail: Academic authors; usual self-evaluation of own system on own benchmark, captured under biases rather than COI.

verdict_reason: Substantive multi-backbone evaluation with a real cost comparison and an honest discussion of metric limits, but the benchmark, verifier, and manual validation are all the authors' own, baselines are under-configured, the 'real' subset is mostly mutations, and nothing is released yet.
applicability: Partly transferable. The Java team's content-delivery services do emit telemetry, and the design lesson holds: put a deterministic localization stage (telemetry diff, then candidate files) in front of a bounded LLM edit and verify against more than tests. That costs about 25x fewer tokens than an open-ended shell agent in this setup. The Java evidence is weak, though: on Train-Ticket Java faults only 32 of 100 patches applied and compiled. Automated incident repair is also far from the team's core needs (ingestion across 4+ repos, spec-driven development). Treat this as a later-stage idea for production incidents, not a harness foundation. Config-repair results (Kubernetes/compose fields) may matter if ingestion pipelines are deployed that way.
